why_how.text: Trucks and buses have huge blind spots, so knowing where they are keeps your car from vanishing from the driver's view.
Motorcyclists usually lose in crashes, so the same alertness that protects them carries over to big vehicles.

scenario.text: Lee is cruising on a highway in the lane beside a tractor-trailer and cannot see the driver's face in its side mirror.

reasoning.text: No face in the mirror means the driver cannot see Lee, and the manual says to pass on the left quickly and get fully ahead.

result.text: Lee speeds up within the limit, passes on the left, and moves fully ahead where the driver can see the car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is safe to follow a truck closely because the driver is high up and can see you.

correction.text: The rear No-Zone can stretch two hundred feet, and a tailgating car is hidden from the driver and cannot see ahead.

memory_support.text: No face in the mirror, no one sees you.

prompt.text: You are directly behind a bus at night. What two things should you do?

answer.text: Stay well back out of the rear No-Zone and dim your headlights.

rationale.text: The rear No-Zone hides a close car, and bright beams reflect off the bus mirrors and blind its driver.

title.text: Sharing the road with big vehicles

lines.text: Motorcyclists usually lose crashes.
Trucks and buses have No-Zones.

narration.text: This lesson moves from motorcycles to the largest vehicles on the road. First, a closing thought on motorcycles: whoever is legally at fault, the motorcyclist is usually the one who loses in a car-motorcycle crash, and alert drivers who watch for riders can reduce those crashes, injuries and deaths. Trucks and buses raise the opposite problem. They are so big that other cars can disappear from the driver's view. The manual calls these danger areas No-Zones, and in this lesson we cover the side and rear ones. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone.

lines.text: Danger areas around trucks and buses.
Some are true blind spots.

narration.text: No-Zones are the areas around trucks and buses where crashes are most likely to happen. Some of them are blind spots, places where your car simply vanishes from the large-vehicle driver's view. That matters because a truck driver who cannot see you may change lanes, brake or turn as if you were not there, especially in an emergency. Learning where the No-Zones are lets you spend as little time in them as possible. There are No-Zones beside, behind and in front of a large vehicle, and around it when it turns or backs up. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone.

lines.text: Big blind spots on both sides.
No face in the mirror means unseen.

narration.text: Trucks and buses have big blind spots on both sides. Here is a simple test: if you cannot see the driver's face in the side mirror, that driver cannot see you either. So do not hang out beside a large vehicle. Pass a truck or bus on the left, and do it as quickly as you can, moving fully ahead of it so the driver can see you. Never cruise alongside it. If the driver needed to change lanes suddenly while you were hidden in the side No-Zone, there would be nowhere for you to go. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone. These are the danger areas where crashes around big vehicles are most likely.

lines.text: Can stretch two hundred feet.
Dim your lights at night.

narration.text: Directly behind a truck or bus is another large No-Zone, one that can stretch as far as two hundred feet. A tailgating car there is hidden from the driver and also cannot see what is happening ahead, so if the big vehicle brakes hard, the car has no escape. Stay well back. At night there is one more rule: dim your headlights whenever you follow a large vehicle, because bright beams bounce off its side mirrors and blind its driver. Staying back and dimming your lights work together to keep both of you safe. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone.

lines.text: Sides: pass quickly on the left.
Rear: do not tailgate at all.

narration.text: Here is where learners mix things up. The side No-Zones and the rear No-Zone call for different responses. Side No-Zones are passed quickly on the left, so you spend as little time hidden as possible. The rear No-Zone, which can reach two hundred feet, is avoided by not tailgating at all, since staying close behind a truck hides you from the driver and blocks your view ahead. A question might suggest riding close behind a truck to stay visible; that is backward. Behind a truck, distance is your protection. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone.

lines.text: Behind a bus at night: what two things?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving directly behind a bus at night. What two things should you do? Settle on your answer, then compare. The answer is to stay well back, out of the rear No-Zone, and to dim your headlights. The rear No-Zone can stretch as far as two hundred feet, and a car inside it is hidden from the driver and cannot see ahead. Bright headlights would bounce off the bus mirrors and blind the driver. Staying back and dimming your lights together protect you and the driver. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone.

lines.text: No face in the mirror, no view of you.
Pass left quickly; never tailgate.

narration.text: To sum up, alert drivers can reduce motorcycle crashes, because the motorcyclist usually loses whoever is at fault. Around trucks and buses, No-Zones are the danger areas where crashes are most likely, and some are blind spots. On the sides, if you cannot see the driver's face in the mirror, the driver cannot see you, so pass on the left quickly and get fully ahead, never cruising alongside. Behind, the No-Zone can stretch two hundred feet, so do not tailgate, and dim your headlights when following a large vehicle at night. Spend as little time as possible in any No-Zone.

why_how.text: Trucks need far more room to stop, so cutting in front of one or misreading its turn can be deadly.

scenario.text: Dana is behind a truck at a corner; the truck swings wide to the left with its right signal blinking, leaving a gap on the right.

reasoning.text: The wide swing is how a truck makes a right turn safely, and passing into the gap on the right is the squeeze play the manual warns about.

result.text: Dana waits behind the truck until the turn is finished instead of slipping into the gap.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a wide gap on a truck's right side is room to pass.

correction.text: The gap opens because the truck swings left to turn right; passing there leaves you unseen and trapped, so wait for the turn to finish.

memory_support.text: Right blinker on a truck, stay behind.

prompt.text: You have just passed a truck on the highway. How do you know it is safe to move back in front of it?

answer.text: When you can see the truck's entire front in your rear-view mirror.

rationale.text: Wait until the whole front shows in your mirror, then move over and keep your speed up so the truck keeps its stopping room.

lines.text: In front, behind a backing truck.
Beside a turning truck.

narration.text: This lesson finishes the No-Zones. You will learn about the front No-Zone, which is about how you move back in after passing; the backing No-Zone behind a truck or bus that is reversing; and the turning No-Zone, which creates a trap called the squeeze play. Along the way you will see why trucks need so much more room to stop than cars, using figures from a study the manual cites. Each of these situations has one clear rule, and mixing them up is a common source of wrong answers and real crashes. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do.

lines.text: Do not cut back in too soon.
Keep your speed up in front.

narration.text: After you pass a large vehicle, do not cut back in too soon. Wait until you can see the truck's entire front in your rear-view mirror before you move over in front of it. Once you are ahead, keep your speed up rather than slowing down. The reason is stopping distance. A truck that suddenly finds a slow car just ahead of its bumper may not be able to stop in time. Giving the truck that full mirror-view gap, and not braking in front of it, keeps the space it needs to slow down safely behind you. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do.

title.text: How far trucks need to stop

lines.text: Nearly twice the room of a car.
Four hundred thirty feet against one ninety-three.

narration.text: Truck and bus drivers need close to twice as much room to stop as car drivers do. The manual backs this up with a National Safety Council study: at fifty-five miles per hour, a loaded truck needs four hundred thirty feet to stop safely, while a passenger car needs one hundred ninety-three feet. That is the nearly double stopping room you must leave a truck. Keep those two figures together, the truck's four hundred thirty and the car's one hundred ninety-three, and you will remember why cutting in front of a truck is so dangerous. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do.

lines.text: Never cross behind a backing truck.
Its driver cannot see directly behind.

narration.text: When a truck or bus is backing up, never cross behind it. Drivers of large vehicles cannot see directly behind their vehicles, and they may not see you at all. Many crashes happen because drivers and pedestrians ignore a backing vehicle and walk or drive into the space behind it. In a parking lot or a loading area, if you see a truck reversing, stop and wait until it has finished or until you can go around it well away from its path. Treat the space directly behind a backing truck as a place you simply do not enter. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do.

lines.text: Trucks swing left to turn right.
Watch the right turn signal.

narration.text: To make a right turn safely, a truck or bus driver has to swing wide to the left first. That swing opens a gap on the truck's right side, and that gap can become a squeeze play. While a large vehicle's right turn signal is blinking, do not try to pass it on the right. The driver cannot see you there, and as the truck completes its turn you could be trapped between it and the curb. The safe choice is to wait behind the truck until it has finished the turn, then continue on your way. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do. In these spaces a large vehicle's driver may not see you at all.

lines.text: Front: no cutting in after passing.
Turning: no passing on the right.

narration.text: Learners often blur two No-Zones. The front No-Zone is about what you do after passing: do not cut in too soon, and wait until the truck's whole front shows in your mirror. The turning No-Zone is about what you do beside a truck that is turning: never pass on the right of a truck signaling a right turn. One is about a gap ahead of the truck, the other about a gap beside it. Both rules come from the same fact, that a large vehicle's driver cannot see you in these spaces and cannot stop or steer as quickly as a car. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do.

lines.text: After passing, when is it safe?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you have just passed a truck on the highway. How do you know it is safe to move back in front of it? Decide first. The answer is that you wait until you can see the truck's entire front in your rear-view mirror, and then move over and keep your speed up. Cutting in sooner, or slowing down once you are in front, takes away the stopping room the truck needs, and trucks need close to twice as much room to stop as cars. The full front in your mirror is your signal that the gap is safe. Trucks need close to twice the room to stop that cars do.

lines.text: Cut in only with the whole front in view.
Never behind a backing truck or right of a turning one.

narration.text: To sum up, after passing a large vehicle, wait until its entire front shows in your rear-view mirror before moving back in, and keep your speed up once you are ahead. Truck and bus drivers need close to twice as much room to stop as car drivers; in the study the manual cites, a loaded truck at fifty-five miles per hour needs four hundred thirty feet against one hundred ninety-three for a car. Never cross behind a backing truck or bus, because its driver cannot see directly behind. And when a truck swings wide left with its right signal blinking, never pass it on the right; wait until the turn is finished.

why_how.text: A car left on the road or a car that rolls on a hill can cause a crash with no driver behind the wheel.

scenario.text: Morgan parks facing downhill on a street with a curb.

reasoning.text: Downhill at a curb, the front wheels turn toward the curb and the car goes in reverse or park, with the hand brake set.

result.text: If the brakes failed, the wheels would roll into the curb instead of into traffic.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the wheels always turn toward the curb, uphill or downhill.

correction.text: Uphill with a curb is the exception: turn the wheels away from the curb and use low gear or park.

memory_support.text: Down to the curb, up away, no curb to the edge.

prompt.text: You park uphill on a street with a curb. Which way do the front wheels turn, and which gear do you use?

answer.text: Away from the curb, in low gear or park.

rationale.text: Uphill at a curb is the only case where the wheels point away from the curb, so the tire can catch the curb if the car rolls back.

lines.text: Standing vehicles on rural highways.
Parking on hills.

narration.text: Parking safely is about more than finding a space. A vehicle left in the wrong place, or one that rolls away, can cause a crash with no one at the wheel. This lesson covers two situations. First, what you must do with any vehicle left standing beside a rural highway, whatever the reason. Second, how to park on a hill so that the car cannot roll into traffic if the brakes fail: the brake and gear routine, and the direction to turn the front wheels when there is a curb and when there is not. Set the hand brake every time you park on a hill. The goal is a car that cannot roll into traffic if the brakes fail.

lines.text: Move it off the traveled part.
If you cannot, use lights and markings.

narration.text: Any vehicle you leave standing beside a rural highway, whatever the reason, has to be moved off the paved or main traveled part of the road. That keeps it out of the path of fast traffic. If the vehicle cannot be moved, for example after a breakdown, you must use lights and markings to warn other traffic that it is there. The rule applies to every reason for stopping, so a short stop does not excuse leaving the car in the lane. Get it off the roadway if you can, and make it clearly visible if you cannot. Set the hand brake every time you park on a hill.

lines.text: Always set the hand brake.
Park, or reverse or low gear.

narration.text: When you park on a hill, you must make sure the car cannot roll into traffic if the brakes do not hold. Always set the hand brake. Then shift into park, or, if the car has no park position, into reverse or low gear. Next, turn the front wheels so that a rolling car would be stopped by the curb or steered off the road. The direction depends on whether you face uphill or downhill and whether there is a curb. Downhill beside a curb, turn the wheels toward the curb and use reverse or park. Set the hand brake every time you park on a hill. The goal is a car that cannot roll into traffic if the brakes fail.

title.text: Uphill at a curb is different

lines.text: Downhill at a curb: toward it.
Uphill at a curb: away from it.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners memorize toward the curb and apply it everywhere. Downhill beside a curb, the wheels do turn toward the curb, with the car in reverse or park. But uphill beside a curb, the front wheels turn away from the curb, and the car goes in low gear or park. Uphill with a curb is the only case where the wheels point away from the curb. Where there is no curb, the wheels turn toward the edge of the road, whether the car faces uphill or downhill, so it would roll away from traffic. Set the hand brake every time you park on a hill.

lines.text: Uphill with a curb: wheels and gear?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you park facing uphill on a street with a curb. Which way do the front wheels turn, and which gear do you use? Work it out first. The answer is away from the curb, with the car in low gear or park, and of course the hand brake set. That is the one case where the wheels point away from the curb. If you said toward the curb, you were thinking of downhill parking at a curb, or of a hill with no curb, where the wheels turn toward the edge of the road. Set the hand brake every time you park on a hill. The goal is a car that cannot roll into traffic if the brakes fail.

lines.text: Brake set; park or a gear.
Down toward, up away, no curb to the edge.

narration.text: To finish, any vehicle left beside a rural highway must be moved off the paved or main traveled part, and if it cannot be moved, lights and markings must warn traffic. On any hill, set the hand brake and shift into park, or into reverse or low gear if there is no park position. Downhill at a curb, turn the wheels toward the curb and use reverse or park. Uphill at a curb, turn them away from the curb and use low gear or park. With no curb, turn the wheels toward the edge of the road, uphill or downhill. Set the hand brake every time you park on a hill.

why_how.text: No-parking rules keep crossings, hydrants and signals clear for the people and vehicles that need them.

scenario.text: Jordan finds an open curb space that is about twenty feet from a fire hydrant and forty feet from a railroad crossing's nearest rail.

reasoning.text: The hydrant gap is fifteen feet, so twenty feet is fine, but parking within fifty feet of the nearest rail is banned.

result.text: Jordan cannot use the space and looks for one at least fifty feet from the rail.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking all no-parking distances are the same.

correction.text: They differ by hazard: fifteen feet from a hydrant, twenty from a crosswalk, thirty from a roadside stop sign or signal, and fifty from the nearest rail.

memory_support.text: Hydrant fifteen, crosswalk twenty, signal thirty, rail fifty.

prompt.text: How close to a stop sign at the side of the road may you park?

rationale.text: Parking is banned within thirty feet of a stop sign, flashing beacon or traffic control signal at the roadside.

lines.text: Some places are always off limits.
Others set a distance.

narration.text: Knowing where you may not park is a test favorite, and the rules come in two kinds. Some places are always off limits, such as intersections, crosswalks, sidewalks, bridges and tunnels. Others set a minimum distance from a hazard, such as a fire hydrant, a crosswalk, a roadside signal or a railroad crossing, and each hazard has its own number. In this lesson you will learn both kinds, plus double parking, yellow curbs and posted signs, and then the steps of parallel parking, so you can fit into a legal space smoothly. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Intersections, crosswalks, sidewalks.
Driveways, bridges, tunnels.

narration.text: You may not park inside an intersection, on a crosswalk, or on a sidewalk. You also may not park in front of a driveway, on any bridge, or inside a tunnel. These places are off limits whatever the time of day and however briefly you plan to stop. Each one either blocks people who need to cross or enter, or leaves your car somewhere that other traffic cannot easily get around it. Think of them as spots where the road or path has to stay open, so a parked car would turn into an obstacle. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Fifteen feet from a fire hydrant.
Twenty feet from a crosswalk.

narration.text: Two of the distance rules are short ones. Parking is banned within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant, so firefighters can reach it. Parking is also banned within twenty feet of a crosswalk at an uncontrolled intersection, so drivers and pedestrians can see each other there. The hydrant distance is the shortest on the list, which makes it easy to mix up with the crosswalk distance. Keep them in order: fifteen for the hydrant, twenty for the crosswalk at an uncontrolled intersection. The next two distances are longer. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Thirty feet from roadside signals.
Fifty feet from the nearest rail.

narration.text: Parking is banned within thirty feet of a stop sign, a flashing beacon or a traffic control signal placed at the roadside, so the sign or signal stays visible to approaching drivers. The longest distance belongs to railroad crossings: parking is banned within fifty feet of the nearest rail. A parked car close to the tracks could block the view of a train or of the crossing itself. So the distances grow with the hazard: fifteen feet for a hydrant, twenty for a crosswalk, thirty for a roadside signal and fifty for the nearest rail. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Pull even with the car ahead.
Ease back, turn sharply, straighten.

narration.text: Once you have found a legal space, parallel park in steps. Pull up even with the parked car ahead of the space. Ease back gently toward the space, then turn the wheels sharply. As the car swings in, begin straightening the wheels, and finish with them parallel to the curb. Doing it in this order keeps the movement smooth and keeps you from hitting the car ahead or the curb. When you pull out again later, remember to look, wait, signal and enter the nearest lane, staying there until a lane change is safe. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Fifteen, twenty, thirty, fifty.
Each belongs to one hazard.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The distances are close enough to blur: fifteen, twenty, thirty and fifty feet. Questions often offer the right number for the wrong hazard. Lock in the pairs: fifteen feet from a fire hydrant, twenty feet from a crosswalk at an uncontrolled intersection, thirty feet from a roadside stop sign, flashing beacon or signal, and fifty feet from the nearest rail of a railroad crossing. If a choice says twenty feet from a hydrant or fifteen from a crosswalk, it has swapped the pair, and you can rule it out. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Stop sign at the roadside: how close?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how close to a stop sign at the side of the road may you park? Decide on your answer first. The answer is no closer than thirty feet. Parking is banned within thirty feet of a stop sign, a flashing beacon or a traffic control signal placed at the roadside. If you were thinking of twenty feet, that is the distance from a crosswalk at an uncontrolled intersection, and fifteen feet is for a fire hydrant. Fifty feet belongs to the nearest rail of a railroad crossing. Check the curb, the signs and the distances before you leave the car.

lines.text: Never in intersections, crosswalks, bridges, tunnels.
Fifteen, twenty, thirty, fifty; then parallel park.

narration.text: To close, never park inside an intersection, on a crosswalk or sidewalk, in front of a driveway, on a bridge or in a tunnel, beside a yellow curb, where signs forbid it, or on the roadway side of a parked car. Keep fifteen feet from a fire hydrant, twenty feet from a crosswalk at an uncontrolled intersection, thirty feet from a roadside stop sign, beacon or signal, and fifty feet from the nearest rail. Then parallel park in steps: pull up even with the car ahead of the space, ease back, turn the wheels sharply, begin straightening, and finish with the wheels parallel to the curb.

why_how.text: The manual calls seat belts the most effective way to reduce serious injuries in traffic crashes.
The child restraint law sets clear stages so every child rides in the right seat.

scenario.text: Pat drives with a three-year-old who weighs thirty pounds and a seven-year-old.

reasoning.text: A forward-facing seat is used until at least five years or forty pounds, and after the booster stage, which ends at six, the law lists a seat belt.

result.text: The three-year-old rides in a forward-facing seat and the seven-year-old wears a seat belt, and both are restrained as the law requires.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the seat belt law only covers the driver and front passenger.

correction.text: Alabama's safety belt law requires every occupant to be restrained, whatever their age, and the child restraint law covers front and back seats.

memory_support.text: One-twenty rear, five-forty forward, six booster, belt to fifteen.

prompt.text: A child has just turned four and weighs thirty-five pounds. Which seat stage applies?

rationale.text: The forward-facing stage lasts until the child is at least five years old or forty pounds, so a four-year-old at thirty-five pounds is still in it.

lines.text: The safety belt law.
The child restraint law.

narration.text: This lesson covers the laws that keep everyone in the car restrained. Alabama's safety belt law requires every occupant to be restrained, no matter their age, and the manual calls wearing seat belts the most effective way to reduce serious injuries in traffic crashes. On top of that, the child restraint law sets size-appropriate seats for children through age fifteen. You will learn how to wear a belt correctly, which vehicles and seats the child law covers, the penalty for breaking it, and the four stages from a rear-facing seat to a seat belt.

lines.text: Every occupant, any age.
Snug across the hip bones.

narration.text: Alabama's safety belt law requires every occupant of the vehicle to be restrained, no matter how old they are. That means the driver and every passenger, in the front and the back. How you wear the belt matters too. A seat belt works best when it is pulled snug across the hip bones, rather than loose or high across the stomach. The manual is clear about why this matters: wearing seat belts is the most effective way to reduce serious injuries in traffic crashes. Buckle up on every trip and make sure everyone else does too. Every occupant, of every age, must be restrained.

lines.text: Children through age fifteen.
Front and back seats; fine and points.

narration.text: Under Alabama's child restraint law, children through age fifteen must be restrained whenever they ride in a motor vehicle in the state. The law covers riders in both the front and back seats of passenger cars, pickup trucks, vans seating ten or fewer, minivans and sport utility vehicles. A driver who breaks the child restraint law pays a fine and also has points put on their driver record. So the responsibility falls on the driver, and a violation affects both your wallet and your record, not just a warning. Every occupant, of every age, must be restrained.

lines.text: Rear-facing, then forward-facing.
Booster, then seat belt.

narration.text: The law sets four size-appropriate stages. An infant rides rear-facing, in an infant-only seat or a convertible seat, until reaching at least one year of age or twenty pounds. Next comes a forward-facing seat, or a convertible seat turned forward, until the child is at least five years of age or forty pounds. A booster seat is then required until the child is six years of age. After the booster stage, the law's size-appropriate system is a seat belt, which it lists until the child is fifteen years of age. Every occupant, of every age, must be restrained.

lines.text: Belt law: every occupant.
Child law: seats through fifteen.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Some learners think the seat belt law only covers adults, or that the child restraint law only covers babies. In fact the safety belt law covers every occupant of any age, while the child restraint law adds size-appropriate seats for children through age fifteen. A second trap is mixing up the stage limits. Rear-facing lasts until at least one year or twenty pounds, forward-facing until at least five years or forty pounds, and the booster seat until six years of age. Keep each number with its stage. Every occupant, of every age, must be restrained.

lines.text: Four years old, thirty-five pounds?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a child has just turned four and weighs thirty-five pounds. Which seat stage applies? Think it through first. The answer is a forward-facing seat. The forward-facing stage lasts until the child is at least five years of age or forty pounds, and this child is younger than five and lighter than forty pounds. The rear-facing stage ends at one year or twenty pounds at the earliest, and the booster seat comes after the forward-facing stage and lasts until age six. Every occupant, of every age, must be restrained. The manual calls seat belts the most effective way to reduce serious crash injuries.

lines.text: Everyone buckles, snug at the hips.
Four stages through age fifteen.

narration.text: To close, Alabama's safety belt law requires every occupant to be restrained, and belts work best snug across the hip bones; the manual calls them the most effective way to reduce serious crash injuries. The child restraint law covers children through age fifteen in front and back seats of cars, pickups, vans seating ten or fewer, minivans and SUVs, and violators pay a fine and get points. The stages run rear-facing to at least one year or twenty pounds, forward-facing to at least five years or forty pounds, booster to six, then a seat belt to fifteen.
